concept: Given an array of daily stock prices, find the maximum profit you can achieve by buying on one day and selling on a later day. If no profit is possible, return zero.

solutions.label: Brute Force
solutions.summary: Check every pair of buy and sell days using nested loops to find the maximum profit.

solutions.label: One-Pass with Running Minimum
solutions.summary: Track the minimum price seen so far and compute the profit at each day in a single pass.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    subgraph Prices["Stock Prices Over 6 Days"]
        D1["Day 1: 7"] --> D2["Day 2: 1"]
        D2 --> D3["Day 3: 5"]
        D3 --> D4["Day 4: 3"]
        D4 --> D5["Day 5: 6"]
        D5 --> D6["Day 6: 4"]
    end
    D2 -. "Buy at 1" .-> B["💰"]
    D5 -. "Sell at 6" .-> B
    B --> R["Profit = 5"]
    style D2 fill:#f87171,color:#fff
    style D5 fill:#f87171,color:#fff
    style R fill:#f87171,color:#fff

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here's the problem. You're given an array of integers where each element represents the stock price on that day. You need to find the maximum profit you can make by choosing one day to buy and a later day to sell. For example, given prices seven, one, five, three, six, four, the answer would be five because you buy at one and sell at six.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Understood. So I must buy before I sell, meaning the buy day must come before the sell day. Can I ask about the input constraints? What's the size range of the array, and are prices always non-negative?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: The array length can be from zero up to one hundred thousand. Prices are non-negative integers. You should return zero if no profit is possible.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: What about edge cases? If the array is empty or has just one element, I can't make any transaction, so I'd return zero. And if prices only decrease, like seven, six, four, one, there's no profitable trade, so also zero. Is that correct?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Exactly right. Those are important edge cases to handle.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Let me summarize. I receive an array of stock prices. I need to pick one buy day and one later sell day to maximize profit. If no profit exists, return zero. I'll start with a brute force solution and then optimize.

sections.title: Brute Force
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    subgraph BF["Brute Force: Check All Pairs"]
        P["Prices: 7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4"]
        P --> C1["i=0,j=1: 1-7 = -6"]
        C1 --> C2["i=0,j=2: 5-7 = -2"]
        C2 --> C3["..."]
        C3 --> C4["i=1,j=2: 5-1 = 4"]
        C4 --> C5["i=1,j=3: 3-1 = 2"]
        C5 --> C6["i=1,j=4: 6-1 = 5 ✓"]
        C6 --> C7["i=1,j=5: 4-1 = 3"]
        C7 --> C8["... remaining pairs"]
        C8 --> R["Max Profit = 5"]
    end
    style C6 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style R fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The simplest approach is to check every possible pair of buy and sell days. I use two nested loops. The outer loop picks the buy day, and the inner loop picks each later sell day. I calculate the difference and keep track of the maximum profit.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Let me walk through the example. With prices seven, one, five, three, six, four, when buy day is index one with price one and sell day is index four with price six, the profit is five. No other pair gives a higher profit.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What's the time complexity of this approach?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Since we compare every pair, the time complexity is O of n-squared, and space is O of one since we only store the maximum profit variable. This works but is slow for large inputs. Can I try to optimize?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes, please go ahead and see if you can do better.

sections.title: One-Pass with Running Minimum
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    subgraph OP["One-Pass: Track Min Price"]
        S["Start: minPrice=7, maxProfit=0"]
        S --> A1["Day 1: price=7, profit=0, min=7"]
        A1 --> A2["Day 2: price=1, new min=1, profit=0"]
        A2 --> A3["Day 3: price=5, profit=5-1=4, max=4"]
        A3 --> A4["Day 4: price=3, profit=3-1=2, max=4"]
        A4 --> A5["Day 5: price=6, profit=6-1=5, max=5 ✓"]
        A5 --> A6["Day 6: price=4, profit=4-1=3, max=5"]
        A6 --> R["Return 5"]
    end
    style A2 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style A5 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style R fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The key insight is that for any sell day, the best buy day is simply the minimum price seen before it. So I can solve this in one pass. I keep a running minimum price and at each step, I check if selling at the current price gives a better profit.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Walking through our example. I start with min price as seven and max profit as zero. At day two, price one becomes the new minimum. At day three, five minus one gives profit four. Day four gives two. Day five, six minus one gives five, which is our new max profit. Day six gives three. Final answer is five.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Nice. What are the time and space complexity now?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Time complexity is O of n because we iterate through the array once. Space complexity is O of one since we only use two variables: the running minimum price and the maximum profit. This is optimal because we must look at every price at least once.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Can you explain why this is sometimes called a sliding window approach?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The minimum price acts as our left pointer and the current day is our right pointer. We're essentially sliding a window from left to right. When we find a new minimum, we move the left boundary. At each step, the window represents the best buy and current sell opportunity.

sections.title: Summary
sections.diagram:
graph LR
    subgraph Comparison["Approach Comparison"]
        BF["Brute Force\nTime: O of n-squared\nSpace: O of 1"]
        OP["One-Pass\nTime: O of n\nSpace: O of 1"]
    end
    BF -- "Optimize" --> OP
    style BF fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style OP fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great job. Let's recap the two approaches.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The brute force checks all pairs in O of n-squared time. The optimized one-pass solution tracks the running minimum and computes profit at each step in O of n time with O of one space. The key takeaway is recognizing that we only need the minimum price before each sell day, which lets us solve it greedily in a single pass.
